why_this_matters: Day 28 sits in Phase 2 (Python for Data Work), whose goal is: Write professional, testable Python that handles real data files, APIs and repos. Today's core material - JSON structures and parsing, Nested JSON to DataFrame, HTML tables with pandas.read_html - is the vocabulary the rest of the phase is built on. Learners who skip the concept and jump to copying code usually stall two weeks later; the goal here is that you can explain what you did, not just that it ran.

code.code:
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
import pandas as pd

url = "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population"

response = requests.get(url)

soup = BeautifulSoup(response.content, "html.parser")

print(soup.title)
print(soup.title.text)

# print(soup.prettify()) # print the whole html code

# find all the tables

tables = soup.find_all("table")

dataframe = [] # empty list

for i, table in enumerate(tables):
    rows = table.find_all("tr")[1:] # skip the first row
    data = [] # empty list
    for row in rows:
        cols = row.find_all("td")
        cols = [col.text.strip() for col in cols]
        data.append(cols)
    df = pd.DataFrame(data)
    dataframe.append(df)
dataframe[1].head()
# dataframe[1].to_csv("world_population.csv", index=False, header=True)

import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
import pandas as pd

# Send a GET request to the Wikipedia page
req = requests.get("https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_population")

# Parse the HTML content using BeautifulSoup
soup = BeautifulSoup(req.content, 'html.parser')

# Find the table containing the population data
table = soup.find('table', {'class': 'wikitable sortable'})

# Find all the rows in the table
rows = table.find_all('tr')

# Create an empty DataFrame to store the data
data = pd.DataFrame(columns=['Rank', 'Country', 'Population'])

# Loop through each row and extract the data
for row in rows:
    # Find all the cells in the row
    cells = row.find_all('td')

    # Extract the data from the cells
    if len(cells) > 1:
        rank = cells[0].text.strip()
        country = cells[1].text.strip()
        population = cells[2].text.strip()

        # Append the data to the DataFrame
        data = pd.concat([data, pd.DataFrame({'Country': [rank], 'Population': [population]})], ignore_index=True)

# Print the DataFrame
data

common_mistakes.mistake: Watching the lecture without running the repository notebook.
common_mistakes.why: Recognition is not recall: code that looked obvious fails the moment you type it yourself.
common_mistakes.fix: For every topic today, run the linked notebook cell, then retype it from memory in your own file.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using JSON structures and parsing on data whose types or shape you have not printed.
common_mistakes.why: Most failures in this topic are input problems (dtype, shape, missing values) rather than logic errors.
common_mistakes.fix: Print type and shape immediately before the operation; keep that habit for all 275 days.

debugging.symptom: The linked notebook cell raises ModuleNotFoundError or ImportError.
debugging.cause: Wrong kernel/environment selected, or the library is not installed in the active environment.
debugging.fix: Print sys.executable in the notebook and install into that environment (Day 4).

debugging.symptom: Your output differs from the recording even though the code looks identical.
debugging.cause: Library version differences, a changed default argument, or unseeded randomness.
debugging.fix: Pin versions (requirements.txt), set a random seed, and compare dtypes and shapes, not just values (Day 5).
